claim: Malaria kills nearly 0.5 million people every year.
source: Malaria is a dangerous mosquito-borne disease which kills nearly 0.5 million of people every year (World Health Organisation, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organisation, 2018

claim: Malaria is caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Plasmodium.
source: It is caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Plasmodium and proceeds in several stages (Miller et al., 2002; Cowman et al., 2012; White et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller et al., 2002; Cowman et al., 2012; White et al., 2014

claim: After about 48 hours post RBC invasion, infected RBCs are ruptured and new merozoites are released into the blood stream.
source: After about 48 hours post RBC invasion, infected RBCs are ruptured and new merozoites are released into the blood stream to repeat this reproduction cycle.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the malaria parasite lifecycle

claim: RBC invasion by merozoites is preceded by three key events: initial attachment, re-orientation or alignment of the parasite, and formation of a tight junction.
source: RBC invasion by merozoites is preceded by three key events: (i) initial attachment, (ii) re-orientation or alignment of the parasite such that its apex is facing the RBC membrane, and (iii) formation of a tight junction (Koch and Baum, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koch and Baum, 2016

claim: The apex contains all required machinery to invade RBCs after the tight junction is formed.
source: The apex contains all required machinery to invade RBCs after the tight junction is formed (Cowman and Crabb, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cowman and Crabb, 2006

claim: Merozoites generally lose their ability to invade RBCs after a couple of minutes.
source: This implies that the parasite alignment is an extremely crucial step for successful invasion, which needs to be completed within a couple of minutes, as after this time period merozoites generally lose their ability to invade RBCs (Crick et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crick et al., 2014

claim: Merozoites contain a surface coat of proteins, mainly GPI-anchored, which can bind to the RBC membrane.
source: To facilitate parasite alignment, merozoites contain a surface coat of proteins, mainly GPI-anchored, which can bind to the RBC membrane (Bannister et al., 1986; Gilson et al., 2006; Beeson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bannister et al., 1986; Gilson et al., 2006; Beeson et al., 2016

claim: Long bonds have a much lower density than short bonds.
source: Furthermore, these long bonds have a much lower density than short bonds.
evidence: This is inferred from electron microscopy observations

claim: Dynamic membrane deformations of various magnitudes are often observed during merozoite alignment.
source: Dynamic membrane deformations of various magnitudes are often observed (Dvorak et al., 1975; Gilson and Crabb, 2009; Glushakova et al., 2005; Crick et al., 2013) and are thought to aid in the alignment process (Weiss et al., 2015; Hillringhaus et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dvorak et al., 1975; Gilson and Crabb, 2009; Glushakova et al., 2005; Crick et al., 2013

claim: There is a positive correlation between RBC deformations and eventual merozoite alignment.
source: Recent live-cell imaging experiments show a positive correlation between RBC deformations and eventual merozoite alignment (Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2015

claim: Calcium release by parasite starts only at the invasion stage.
source: This proposition has been confronted by recent experiments (Introini et al., 2018), which show that calcium release by parasite starts only at the invasion stage.
evidence: Supported by citation to Introini et al., 2018

claim: The merozoite is considered to be a rigid body.
source: The parasite is much less deformable than the RBC, as no deformations of parasite body are visible in experiments (Weiss et al., 2015; Crick et al., 2014). Therefore, the merozoite is considered to be a rigid body, whose dynamics can be described by equations involving force and torque on the parasite's center of mass and directional vector (Heard, 2006).
evidence: Based on experimental observations from Weiss et al., 2015; Crick et al., 2014 and modeling approach from Heard, 2006

claim: Simulated fixed-time displacements of the parasite at RBC membrane are calibrated against experimental distribution.
source: By adapting the interaction parameters, the displacement distribution in simulations is calibrated against the experimental distribution.
evidence: Figure 2b shows comparison between experimental and simulated fixed-time displacements

claim: For shorter timescales, the MSD of parasite motion shows a transient anomalous subdiffusion.
source: For shorter timescales, the MSD of parasite motion shows a transient anomalous subdiffusion, which may occur, for instance, in the case of sticky particle dynamics with alterations between sticking (i.e., stopping its motion for some time) and diffusing states (Saxton, 2007; Höfling and Franosch, 2013).
evidence: Based on mean squared displacement analysis shown in Figure 2c, with theoretical support from Saxton, 2007; Höfling and Franosch, 2013

claim: A successful alignment occurs more frequently in the concave areas of RBC dimples than at the convex rim of the membrane.
source: A further noteworthy result from simulations is that a successful alignment occurs more frequently in the concave areas of RBC dimples than at the convex rim of the membrane.
evidence: Based on simulation results

claim: The merozoite forms more bonds in the dimples than at the RBC rim.
source: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows that the merozoite forms more bonds in the dimples than at the RBC rim, confirming the position-dependent differences in membrane wrapping.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: There is a clear correlation between the level of membrane deformations and average alignment time.
source: Figure 6b,c shows that there is a clear correlation between the level of membrane deformations and average alignment time.
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 6b,c

claim: Bonds with a larger rigidity lead to the formation of a larger number of bonds, more membrane wrapping, and a larger RBC deformation energy in comparison to soft bonds.
source: Bonds with a larger rigidity lead to the formation of a larger number of bonds, more membrane wrapping, and a larger RBC deformation energy in comparison to soft bonds.
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 7

claim: Larger RBC rigidity leads to much longer parasite alignment times.
source: Clearly, larger RBC rigidity leads to much longer parasite alignment times (see Figure 9b), emphasizing again the importance of membrane deformations for merozoite alignment.
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 9b

claim: The displacement at the rigid membrane is larger than at the flexible membrane.
source: However, the displacement at the rigid membrane is larger than at the flexible membrane (for visual comparison, see Videos 1 and 3), because the merozoite forms less bonds at the rigid surface.
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 9a

claim: The presented model is able to reproduce quantitatively experimentally measured alignment times.
source: The presented model is able to reproduce quantitatively experimentally measured alignment times.
evidence: Based on comparison between simulation and experimental results

claim: Parasite alignment is mediated by RBC membrane deformations and a diffusive-like dynamics due to the stochastic nature of parasite-membrane interactions.
source: Our main result is that parasite alignment is mediated by RBC membrane deformations and a diffusive-like dynamics due to the stochastic nature of parasite-membrane interactions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the simulation study

claim: Membrane deformations speed up the alignment through partial wrapping of the parasite, facilitating a contact between the parasite apex and the membrane.
source: Our results show that membrane deformations speed up the alignment through partial wrapping of the parasite, facilitating a contact between the parasite apex and the membrane.
evidence: Based on simulation results

claim: Simulations of parasite alignment at a rigid RBC show a drastic increase in alignment times.
source: The importance of membrane deformation is also corroborated by simulations of parasite alignment at a rigid RBC, which show a drastic increase in alignment times.
evidence: Based on simulation results

claim: Infected RBCs in malaria become significantly stiffer than healthy cells.
source: For example, infected RBCs in malaria become significantly stiffer than healthy cells (Suresh et al., 2005; Fedosov et al., 2011), limiting secondary invasion events.
evidence: Supported by citations to Suresh et al., 2005; Fedosov et al., 2011

claim: The model is able to explain the possibility of RBC invasion by a merozoite without preceding membrane deformations.
source: Therefore, our model is also able to explain the possibility of RBC invasion by a merozoite without preceding membrane deformations, which is observed much less frequently than the invasion preceded by significant RBC deformations (Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on simulation results and comparison with experiments from Weiss et al., 2015

claim: The bond-based model is more appropriate for the representation of RBC-parasite interactions than the potential-based model.
source: Thus, the bond-based model is more appropriate for the representation of RBC-parasite interactions.
evidence: Based on comparison between bond-based and potential-based models

claim: Long bonds serve as leverages for stable parasite adhesion and its motion at the membrane.
source: Therefore, the long bonds serve as leverages for stable parasite adhesion and its motion at the membrane.
evidence: Based on simulation results

claim: The model suggests that the parasite alignment can be explained by the passive compliance hypothesis.
source: In conclusion, our model suggests that the parasite alignment can be explained by the passive compliance hypothesis (Introini et al., 2018; Hillringhaus et al., 2019), such that no additional active mechanisms or processes are necessary.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study, with references to Introini et al., 2018; Hillringhaus et al., 2019
